sahneler.alt: Site of loss, air conduction, bone conduction and the gap
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In earlier lessons, we learned to read an audiogram and followed the journey of sound through the ear.
In this lesson, we classify hearing loss by its site and learn to tell conductive, sensorineural and mixed loss apart on the audiogram.
The most basic way to classify hearing loss is to ask where along the auditory pathway the problem lies.
If the problem is in the outer or middle ear, sound is not conducted well to the inner ear; this is conductive hearing loss.
If the problem is in the inner ear, that is, the cochlea, or in the auditory nerve, it is called sensorineural hearing loss.
The term sensorineural has two parts: sensory, meaning cochlear, and neural, meaning related to the nerve.
If there is a problem in both parts, the loss is mixed.
This classification tells us not how much loss there is, but where it is.
So the three types of hearing loss by site are conductive, sensorineural and mixed hearing loss.

yan.metin: Air conduction threshold minus *bone conduction* threshold

cumleler: The key to finding the type is to compare the two test routes on the audiogram.
The air conduction threshold tests the outer, middle and inner ear all together.
The bone conduction threshold largely bypasses the conductive system and shows the sensitivity of the cochlea.
When we subtract the bone conduction threshold from the air conduction threshold at the same frequency, we get the air-bone gap.
In clinical reports, this concept is simply called the air-bone gap.
A gap greater than ten decibels, that is, fifteen decibels or more, is usually considered significant.
If air and bone conduction are within normal limits and there is no gap, hearing is normal.
If bone conduction is normal, air conduction is reduced and the gap is significant, the loss is conductive.
If air and bone conduction are reduced together and there is no gap, the loss is sensorineural.
If bone conduction is reduced and a significant gap is added on top, the loss is mixed.
These four lines sum up the basic logic of finding the type.
In this sample audiogram, the air conduction thresholds of the right ear are between thirty five and forty five decibels.
The bone conduction thresholds are between five and ten decibels, which is within normal limits.
At five hundred hertz, the air-bone gap is thirty decibels, and at the other frequencies it is twenty five to thirty five decibels.
This is a conductive hearing loss: the cochlea works well, but sound cannot be fully conducted to it.
In conductive losses, the curve is often flat or slightly worse in the low frequencies.
In conductive loss, bone conduction is within normal limits.
The loss usually does not exceed about sixty decibels, because louder sounds reach the cochlea through the skull anyway.
So a profound loss is not expected to be explained by a conductive component alone.
When sound is made loud enough, speech understanding is usually good.
Example causes include earwax blocking the canal, middle ear fluid, a perforated tympanic membrane, and otosclerosis.
Some of these losses can be corrected medically or surgically; this assessment belongs to the ENT physician.
In this example, the air conduction thresholds of the left ear get steadily worse toward the high frequencies.
The bone conduction thresholds closely follow air conduction.
At every frequency, the difference between the two routes is at most five decibels, so there is no significant air-bone gap.
The conductive system carries sound well, but the cochlea or the nerve picks it up poorly.
This is an example of a sloping sensorineural hearing loss, a common pattern in adults.
Sensorineural loss can be divided into two groups.
In sensory, or cochlear, loss, the problem is usually in the hair cells.
In this case, otoacoustic emissions, or OAEs, which depend on the outer hair cells, are usually reduced or absent.
Noise-induced and age-related hearing loss are examples of cochlear loss.
In neural, or retrocochlear, loss, the problem is in the auditory nerve or the brainstem.
In this case, the auditory brainstem response, or ABR, may be abnormal.
Vestibular schwannoma, a benign tumor that grows on the vestibulocochlear nerve, is an example of this group.
The audiogram alone cannot separate these two; tests such as OAE and ABR are needed.
In sensorineural loss, air and bone conduction thresholds drop together.
It can occur at any degree, from mild to total loss.
These people often say they can hear sound but struggle to understand it, especially in noisy places.
This is because a damaged cochlea not only weakens sound but also blurs frequency resolution.
Most sensorineural losses are permanent; for these people, hearing aids and implants are key rehabilitation options.
A sudden sensorineural loss, however, is an emergency, and the person is referred to a physician right away.
Now let us look at a mixed example from a right ear.
The air conduction thresholds are between fifty five and seventy five decibels.
The bone conduction thresholds are between thirty and forty five decibels, so bone conduction is not normal either.
On top of that, there is a gap of about twenty five decibels between the two routes at each frequency.
The drop in bone conduction shows the sensorineural component, and the gap shows the conductive component.
In this example, part of the loss comes from the inner ear and part from the conductive system.
When reading a mixed loss, we describe the two components separately; bone conduction shows the sensorineural level.
The size of the conductive component is shown by the air-bone gap.
A report might say, for example: moderately severe mixed hearing loss in the right ear.
Long-standing middle ear disease and advanced otosclerosis are examples of conditions that can cause a mixed loss.
Even if the conductive component is removed, the sensorineural component shown by bone conduction usually remains.
Some situations can mislead us when we determine the type.
Bone-conducted sound reaches both cochleae; without masking, the response may come from the better ear.
With supra-aural earphones, the ear canal collapses in some people, creating a false air-bone gap in the high frequencies.
The output of the bone vibrator is limited, so in severe losses there may be no bone conduction response.
In severe losses, feeling low-frequency vibration as touch can also create a false gap.
In otosclerosis, bone conduction may dip around two thousand hertz; this is called the Carhart notch.
This notch is not a true cochlear loss, and it usually improves after surgery.
The type seen on the audiogram is confirmed with other tests; this is called the cross-check principle.
Otoscopy shows the ear canal and the tympanic membrane directly.
Tympanometry measures middle ear mobility and gives abnormal results in most conductive losses.
Acoustic reflexes are usually absent even with a small conductive component.
Otoacoustic emissions and the ABR help separate the cochlear and neural parts.

sahneler.metin: With an unexpected air-bone gap, first check otoscopy, earphone placement and masking. Insert earphones prevent the collapsed canal problem.
cumleler: A practical tip: when you see an unexpected air-bone gap, do not write conductive loss straight away.
First, use otoscopy to check the ear canal and the tympanic membrane.
Then check whether the earphones were placed correctly and whether enough masking was used for bone conduction.
If you suspect a collapsing ear canal, repeating the test with insert earphones often solves the problem.
The tympanometry result is also a good way to check whether the gap is consistent.

maddeler.metin: A gap of 15 dB or *more*: significant

cumleler: By site, hearing loss is classified as conductive, sensorineural or mixed.
Bone conduction largely bypasses the conductive system and shows the state of the cochlea.
A difference of fifteen decibels or more between air and bone conduction is a significant air-bone gap.
We confirm the type on the audiogram with otoscopy, tympanometry, reflexes, OAE and ABR.

sahneler.soru: Air conduction is 60 and bone conduction 35 dB HL. What type of loss is this?
sahneler.aciklama: Bone conduction is not normal (_sensorineural component_) and there is a 25 dB gap (conductive component): mixed.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: If air conduction is sixty and bone conduction is thirty five dB HL, what type of loss is it?

cumleler: The correct answer is C, mixed. Bone conduction is not normal, and a twenty five decibel air-bone gap is added on top.
